items.stem: What is electrolysis?
options: the movement of electrons through a metal wire
the dissolving of an ionic compound in water
the decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current
the reaction of a metal with an acid
items.answer: the decomposition of an ionic compound, when molten or in aqueous solution, by the passage of an electric current
items.markingKey: Definition of electrolysis.

items.stem: Explain why solid lead(II) bromide does not conduct electricity but molten lead(II) bromide does.
items.answer: In the solid the ions are held in fixed positions in the lattice; when molten the ions can move to the electrodes and carry the charge.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: solid ions fixed; 1 mark: molten ions mobile [2]

items.stem: Describe how charge is carried in the external circuit and in the electrolyte during electrolysis.
items.answer: Electrons flow through the external wires; ions move through the electrolyte (cations to the cathode, anions to the anode).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: electrons in wires; 1 mark: ions in electrolyte [2]

items.stem: Write the ionic half-equation for the formation of magnesium at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten magnesium chloride.
items.answer: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg
items.markingKey: Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg: species [1]; electrons balanced [1]

items.stem: Molten lead(II) iodide, PbI₂, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. Name the products at each electrode and write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at each electrode.
items.answer: cathode: lead, Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb; anode: iodine, 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: cathode: lead [1]; Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb [1]; anode: iodine [1]; 2I⁻ → I₂ + 2e⁻ [1]

items.stem: Freya electrolyses molten sodium chloride, NaCl, using graphite electrodes. (a) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode. (c) Identify which electrode reaction is reduction, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na (b) 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (c) cathode: metal ions gain electrons

items.stem: What is the name of the negative electrode?
items.answer: cathode
items.markingKey: Cathode = negative; cations are attracted to it.

items.stem: Explain why a metal is always formed at the cathode when a molten binary ionic compound is electrolysed.
items.answer: The metal ions are positive, so they are attracted to the negative cathode, where they gain electrons and become metal atoms.

items.stem: Explain why electrolysis of molten lead(II) bromide should be done in a fume cupboard.
items.answer: Bromine vapour is produced at the anode and it is toxic.

items.stem: Explain the meaning of the term binary compound in "molten binary ionic compound".
items.answer: A compound made of only two elements, such as a metal and a non-metal (e.g. NaCl).

items.stem: Write the ionic half-equation for the formation of lead at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten lead(II) iodide.
items.answer: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb
items.markingKey: Pb²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Pb: species [1]; electrons balanced [1]

items.stem: Molten lithium bromide, LiBr, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. Name the products at each electrode and write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at each electrode.
items.answer: cathode: lithium, Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li; anode: bromine, 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: cathode: lithium [1]; Li⁺ + e⁻ → Li [1]; anode: bromine [1]; 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ [1]

items.stem: Yusuf electrolyses molten lithium bromide, LiBr, using graphite electrodes. (a) Explain why the compound must be molten. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode. (c) Identify which electrode reaction is reduction, giving a reason. (d) Describe the movement of electrons in the external circuit.
items.answer: (a) so that the ions are free to move to the electrodes (b) 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (c) cathode: metal ions gain electrons (d) from the anode through the wires to the cathode (via the power supply)

items.stem: Which ions are present in all aqueous solutions, in addition to the ions of the dissolved compound?
items.answer: H⁺ and OH⁻
items.markingKey: Water ionises slightly: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻.

items.stem: Explain why hydrogen, not sodium, is produced at the cathode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed.
items.answer: Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions (from water) gain electrons more readily than Na⁺ ions; hydrogen gas forms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Na more reactive than H; 1 mark: H⁺ discharged [2]

items.stem: Explain why the blue colour of copper(II) sulfate solution fades during electrolysis with inert electrodes.
items.answer: Cu²⁺ ions, which cause the blue colour, are removed from solution as copper is deposited on the cathode.

items.stem: Ines electrolyses aqueous copper(II) sulfate using graphite electrodes. List the ions present in the solution and predict the product at each electrode, explaining your predictions.
items.answer: Ions: Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻. Cathode: copper – copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ ions are discharged. Anode: oxygen – there are no halide ions, so OH⁻ ions are discharged to give oxygen.
items.markingKey: ions Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ [1]; cathode copper with reason [1]; anode oxygen with reason [1]

items.stem: Aqueous sodium sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which observation identifies the product at the cathode?
options: A pink-brown solid coats the cathode.
A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
The solution near the anode turns brown.
items.answer: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
items.markingKey: Cathode product: hydrogen – a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: Arjun electrolyses concentrated aqueous potassium bromide using graphite electrodes. List the ions present in the solution and predict the product at each electrode, explaining your predictions. Write the half-equation at each electrode and describe a test for each product.
items.answer: Ions: K⁺, Br⁻, H⁺, OH⁻. Cathode: hydrogen – the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead. Anode: bromine – halide ions in a concentrated solution are discharged. 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂; 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻. Tests: hydrogen – a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop; bromine – the solution near the anode turns orange/brown.
items.markingKey: ions K⁺, Br⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ [1]; cathode hydrogen with reason [1]; anode bromine with reason [1]; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ [1]; 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ [1]; tests [1]

items.stem: A technician in Muscat electrolyses concentrated aqueous potassium bromide with carbon electrodes and collects the products. (a) List all the ions present in the solution. (b) Name the product at the cathode and explain why it forms. (c) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode.
items.answer: (a) K⁺, Br⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ (b) hydrogen: the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead (c) 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark product; 1 mark reason [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: A technician in Kuala Lumpur electrolyses aqueous copper(II) sulfate with carbon electrodes and collects the products. (a) List all the ions present in the solution. (b) Name the product at the anode and explain why it forms. (c) Describe a test to identify the product at the anode. (d) Describe one change in the electrolyte during the experiment.
items.answer: (a) Cu²⁺, SO₄²⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ (b) oxygen: there are no halide ions, so OH⁻ ions are discharged to give oxygen (c) a glowing splint relights (d) the blue colour fades and the solution becomes acidic
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark product; 1 mark reason [2] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: What forms at the cathode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed?
items.answer: hydrogen
items.markingKey: Na is more reactive than H, so H⁺ is discharged.

items.stem: Explain why the solution becomes alkaline during the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride.
items.answer: H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are removed; Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain, forming sodium hydroxide.

items.stem: Explain why the volume of hydrogen collected is twice the volume of oxygen when dilute sulfuric acid is electrolysed.
items.answer: For every 4 electrons, 2 H₂ are formed at the cathode (4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂) but only 1 O₂ at the anode (4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻).

items.stem: Explain why oxygen, not chlorine, may be the main product at the anode when very dilute aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed.
items.answer: In a dilute solution the concentration of Cl⁻ ions is low, so OH⁻ ions are discharged instead, giving oxygen.

items.stem: Explain why hydrogen is produced at the cathode when aqueous potassium nitrate is electrolysed.
items.answer: Positive ions present are K⁺, H⁺; the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies cations present; 1 mark: reactivity reasoning [2]

items.stem: Aqueous copper(II) sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which observation identifies the product at the anode?
options: Damp blue litmus paper turns red then is bleached white.
The solution near the anode turns brown.
A pink-brown solid coats the cathode.
items.answer: A glowing splint relights.
items.markingKey: Anode product: oxygen – a glowing splint relights.

items.stem: Isla electrolyses aqueous potassium nitrate using graphite electrodes. List the ions present in the solution and predict the product at each electrode, explaining your predictions.
items.answer: Ions: K⁺, NO₃⁻, H⁺, OH⁻. Cathode: hydrogen – the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead. Anode: oxygen – there are no halide ions, so OH⁻ ions are discharged to give oxygen.
items.markingKey: ions K⁺, NO₃⁻, H⁺, OH⁻ [1]; cathode hydrogen with reason [1]; anode oxygen with reason [1]

items.stem: Jonas electrolyses aqueous sodium hydroxide using graphite electrodes. List the ions present in the solution and predict the product at each electrode, explaining your predictions.
items.answer: Ions: Na⁺, OH⁻, H⁺. Cathode: hydrogen – the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead. Anode: oxygen – there are no halide ions, so OH⁻ ions are discharged to give oxygen.
items.markingKey: ions Na⁺, OH⁻, H⁺ [1]; cathode hydrogen with reason [1]; anode oxygen with reason [1]

items.stem: Mateo sets up a cell to electrolyse aqueous silver nitrate using inert graphite electrodes. (a) Name the product at the cathode and explain why it forms. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. (c) Describe a test to identify the product at the anode. (d) Describe one change in the electrolyte during the experiment.
items.answer: (a) silver: silver is less reactive than hydrogen, so Ag⁺ ions are discharged (b) Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag (c) a glowing splint relights (d) the concentration of the dissolved compound changes as ions are discharged
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark product; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [1] (c) [1] (d) [1]

items.stem: Lina sets up a cell to electrolyse aqueous copper(II) sulfate using inert graphite electrodes. (a) Name the product at the cathode and explain why it forms. (b) Describe a test to identify the product at the anode. (c) Describe one change in the electrolyte during the experiment.
items.answer: (a) copper: copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ ions are discharged (b) a glowing splint relights (c) the blue colour fades and the solution becomes acidic
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark product; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: In electroplating, where is the object to be plated placed?
items.answer: as the cathode
items.markingKey: Metal ions gain electrons and deposit on the cathode.

items.stem: Explain why the concentration of copper(II) ions in the electrolyte stays constant during the purification of copper.
items.answer: Copper atoms at the anode lose electrons and go into solution as Cu²⁺ at the same rate as Cu²⁺ ions gain electrons and are deposited at the cathode.

items.stem: Explain what happens to the impurities in the impure copper anode during purification.
items.answer: Insoluble impurities (e.g. silver, gold) fall to the bottom as anode sludge; more reactive metals dissolve as ions and stay in solution.

items.stem: A brass medal is to be electroplated with silver. Name the anode, the cathode and a suitable electrolyte.
items.answer: anode: silver; cathode: brass medal; electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Isla wants to electroplate a steel spoon with silver. Describe the set-up: name the anode, the cathode and the electrolyte, and write the half-equations at each electrode.
items.answer: anode: silver; cathode: the steel spoon; electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate. Cathode: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag; anode: Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻
items.markingKey: anode silver [1]; cathode steel spoon [1]; electrolyte silver nitrate [1]; Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag [1]; anode half-equation [1]

items.stem: Aisha sets up a cell to purify a bar of impure copper by electrolysis. (a) Name the anode, cathode and electrolyte used. (b) Suggest why very pure copper is needed for wiring.
items.answer: (a) anode: impure copper; cathode: pure copper; electrolyte: aqueous copper(II) sulfate (b) impurities reduce electrical conductivity
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Explain why the electrolyte in electroplating must contain ions of the plating metal.
items.answer: These ions are discharged (gain electrons) at the cathode to form the metal coating; the anode of the same metal replaces them.

items.stem: Explain why a copper anode gets smaller when copper(II) sulfate solution is electrolysed using copper electrodes.
items.answer: Copper atoms at the anode are oxidised to Cu²⁺ ions (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻), which pass into solution.

items.stem: Jonas tried to electroplate a steel bicycle bell with nickel but used aqueous sodium chloride as the electrolyte. Explain why this would not work well and how to correct it.
items.answer: The electrolyte must contain Ni²⁺ ions (e.g. nickel(II) sulfate); with NaCl, hydrogen would form at the cathode instead of nickel.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: problem explained; 1 mark: correction [2]

items.stem: A iron key is to be electroplated with copper. Name the anode, the cathode and a suitable electrolyte.
items.answer: anode: copper; cathode: iron key; electrolyte: aqueous copper(II) sulfate
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Isla purifies copper by electrolysis. During the experiment the impure copper anode loses 5.60 g and the pure copper cathode gains 5.46 g. Calculate the percentage of copper in the impure anode and explain why the two masses are different.
items.answer: 97.5%; the anode also contained impurities, which fell as sludge or dissolved without being deposited.
items.markingKey: % = 5.46 ÷ 5.60 × 100 [1] = 97.5% [1]; impurities lost from anode do not deposit on cathode [1]

items.stem: Chloe sets up a cell to purify a bar of impure copper by electrolysis. (a) Write the half-equation at the anode. (b) Describe what happens to the impurities. (c) Suggest why very pure copper is needed for wiring.
items.answer: (a) Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ (b) unreactive metals fall as anode sludge; reactive metals dissolve and stay in solution (c) impurities reduce electrical conductivity

items.stem: Copper used for electrical wiring must be very pure. Priya visits a refinery in Lisbon where impure copper is purified by electrolysis. (a) Write the half-equation at the cathode. (b) Explain why the colour of the electrolyte does not change. (c) Describe what happens to the impurities. (d) Suggest why very pure copper is needed for wiring.
items.answer: (a) Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (b) Cu²⁺ ions are added at the anode at the same rate they are removed at the cathode (c) unreactive metals fall as anode sludge; reactive metals dissolve and stay in solution (d) impurities reduce electrical conductivity

items.stem: What is the only chemical product of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell?
items.answer: water
items.markingKey: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.

items.stem: What does a fuel cell produce directly from chemical energy?
items.answer: electrical energy
items.markingKey: A fuel cell uses hydrogen and oxygen to produce electricity.

items.stem: Explain why hydrogen fuel cell cars are described as "zero emission" but may still contribute to climate change.
items.answer: At the point of use only water is produced; but if the hydrogen is made from fossil fuels (e.g. methane) or the electricity for electrolysis comes from fossil fuels, CO₂ is released during production.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: only water in use; 1 mark: CO₂ from hydrogen production [2]

items.stem: Mei compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a petrol car in Colombo. Data: range on a full tank – fuel cell 480 km, petrol 800 km; refuelling time – fuel cell 4 min, petrol 5 min; CO₂ emitted while driving – fuel cell 0 g/km, petrol 180 g/km; purchase price – fuel cell $55,000, petrol $30,000; filling stations in the city – hydrogen 5, petrol 800. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the fuel cell car shown by the data, and state which car you would choose.
items.answer: Fuel cell: no CO₂ or other pollutants when driving (only water), but costs $25,000 more, has 320 km less range and there are only 5 hydrogen filling stations; hydrogen may be made from fossil fuels. Petrol: cheaper, convenient, but emits CO₂ (climate change) plus CO, NOx and particulates. A justified conclusion either way.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one advantage from the data; 1 mark: one disadvantage from the data; 1 mark: conclusion with reason [3]

items.stem: A city council in Seoul is replacing petrol vans with hydrogen fuel cell vans. (a) State the energy change that takes place in a fuel cell. (b) Give two advantages of fuel cell vans compared with petrol vans.
items.answer: (a) chemical energy → electrical energy (b) the only chemical product is water, so no carbon dioxide or other pollutants are released at the point of use; fuel cells are more efficient at converting chemical energy to electrical energy
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell car compared with a petrol car?
options: It produces no carbon dioxide when running.
Fuel cells are cheap to make.
There are many hydrogen filling stations.
items.answer: It produces no carbon dioxide when running.
items.markingKey: Water is the only product.

items.stem: Zara compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a petrol car in Bogotá. Data: range on a full tank – fuel cell 480 km, petrol 800 km; refuelling time – fuel cell 6 min, petrol 3 min; CO₂ emitted while driving – fuel cell 0 g/km, petrol 160 g/km; purchase price – fuel cell $65,000, petrol $25,000; filling stations in the city – hydrogen 8, petrol 1500. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the fuel cell car shown by the data, and state which car you would choose.
items.answer: Fuel cell: no CO₂ or other pollutants when driving (only water), but costs $40,000 more, has 320 km less range and there are only 8 hydrogen filling stations; hydrogen may be made from fossil fuels. Petrol: cheaper, convenient, but emits CO₂ (climate change) plus CO, NOx and particulates. A justified conclusion either way.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one advantage from the data; 1 mark: one disadvantage from the data; 1 mark: conclusion with reason [3]

items.stem: Felix researches hydrogen–oxygen fuel cells for a school project. (a) Write the overall equation for the reaction in the fuel cell. (b) State the energy change that takes place in a fuel cell. (c) Name two pollutants produced by petrol engines that are not produced by fuel cells.
items.answer: (a) 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (b) chemical energy → electrical energy (c) carbon dioxide; carbon monoxide (also oxides of nitrogen, particulates)

items.stem: Why must lead(II) bromide be molten before it can be electrolysed?
options: The electrons must be free to move.
The bromine must be a gas.
The ions must be free to move.
items.answer: The ions must be free to move.

items.stem: Explain how lithium and bromine are formed at the electrodes when molten lithium bromide is electrolysed. Refer to the movement of ions and electrons.
items.answer: Li⁺ ions move to the cathode (negative) and gain electrons to form lithium; Br⁻ ions move to the anode (positive) and lose electrons to form bromine. Electrons flow through the external circuit from anode to cathode.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cations to cathode gain electrons; 1 mark: anions to anode lose electrons; total [2]

items.stem: Write the ionic half-equation for the formation of zinc at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten zinc chloride.
items.answer: Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn

(b) Describe what happens to the impurities. (c) The anode loses 5.00 g and the cathode gains 4.80 g. Calculate the percentage purity of the copper anode. (d) Suggest why very pure copper is needed for wiring.
items.answer: (a) Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (b) unreactive metals fall as anode sludge; reactive metals dissolve and stay in solution (c) 96.0% (d) impurities reduce electrical conductivity

items.stem: Compare the products of combustion in a petrol engine with the products of a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell.
items.answer: Petrol engine: carbon dioxide, water, and pollutants such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides and particulates; fuel cell: water only.

items.stem: Explain why storing hydrogen is a problem for fuel cell vehicles.
items.answer: Hydrogen is a gas with a low density, so it must be stored at very high pressure in heavy, strong tanks; it is also highly flammable.

items.stem: Tomás compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a petrol car in Dubai. Data: range on a full tank – fuel cell 550 km, petrol 650 km; refuelling time – fuel cell 5 min, petrol 4 min; CO₂ emitted while driving – fuel cell 0 g/km, petrol 160 g/km; purchase price – fuel cell $55,000, petrol $35,000; filling stations in the city – hydrogen 8, petrol 2000. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the fuel cell car shown by the data, and state which car you would choose.
items.answer: Fuel cell: no CO₂ or other pollutants when driving (only water), but costs $20,000 more, has 100 km less range and there are only 8 hydrogen filling stations; hydrogen may be made from fossil fuels. Petrol: cheaper, convenient, but emits CO₂ (climate change) plus CO, NOx and particulates. A justified conclusion either way.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one advantage from the data; 1 mark: one disadvantage from the data; 1 mark: conclusion with reason [3]

items.stem: Which product forms at the anode when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed?
items.answer: chlorine
items.markingKey: Cl⁻ ions are attracted to the anode and lose electrons.

items.stem: Explain how sodium and chlorine are formed at the electrodes when molten sodium chloride is electrolysed. Refer to the movement of ions and electrons.
items.answer: Na⁺ ions move to the cathode (negative) and gain electrons to form sodium; Cl⁻ ions move to the anode (positive) and lose electrons to form chlorine. Electrons flow through the external circuit from anode to cathode.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: cations to cathode gain electrons; 1 mark: anions to anode lose electrons; total [2]

items.stem: Write the ionic half-equation for the formation of sodium at the cathode during the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.
items.answer: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na
items.markingKey: Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na: species [1]; electrons balanced [1]

items.stem: Molten zinc chloride, ZnCl₂, is electrolysed using graphite electrodes. Name the products at each electrode and write the ionic half-equation for the reaction at each electrode.
items.answer: cathode: zinc, Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn; anode: chlorine, 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻
items.markingKey: cathode: zinc [1]; Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Zn [1]; anode: chlorine [1]; 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ [1]

items.stem: In an industrial process in Doha, molten magnesium chloride, MgCl₂, is electrolysed using inert electrodes. (a) Explain why the compound must be molten. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. (c) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode. (d) Describe the movement of electrons in the external circuit.
items.answer: (a) so that the ions are free to move to the electrodes (b) Mg²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Mg (c) 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻ (d) from the anode through the wires to the cathode (via the power supply)

items.stem: Which test identifies the gas produced at the anode when concentrated hydrochloric acid is electrolysed?
options: It gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint.
items.answer: It bleaches damp litmus paper.
items.markingKey: Chlorine bleaches damp litmus.

items.stem: Explain why copper is produced at the cathode when concentrated aqueous copper(II) chloride is electrolysed.
items.answer: Positive ions present are Cu²⁺, H⁺; copper is less reactive than hydrogen, so Cu²⁺ ions are discharged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies cations present; 1 mark: reactivity reasoning [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why hydrogen, not sodium, is produced at the cathode when concentrated aqueous sodium chloride is electrolysed. (b) Explain why the solution becomes alkaline during the electrolysis of concentrated aqueous sodium chloride.
items.answer: (a) Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions (from water) gain electrons more readily than Na⁺ ions; hydrogen gas forms. (b) H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions are removed; Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions remain, forming sodium hydroxide.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: Na more reactive than H; 1 mark: H⁺ discharged [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Concentrated aqueous copper(II) bromide is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which observation identifies the product at the cathode?
options: The solution near the anode turns brown.
A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
A pink-brown solid coats the cathode.
The solution near the anode turns orange/brown.
items.answer: A pink-brown solid coats the cathode.
items.markingKey: Cathode product: copper – a pink-brown solid coats the cathode.

items.stem: Aqueous magnesium sulfate is electrolysed with inert electrodes. Which observation identifies the product at the cathode?
options: A pink-brown solid coats the cathode.
Damp blue litmus paper turns red then is bleached white.
A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
items.answer: A lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
items.markingKey: Cathode product: hydrogen – a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.

items.stem: Sipho sets up a cell to electrolyse aqueous sodium hydroxide using inert graphite electrodes. (a) List all the ions present in the solution. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. (c) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode. (d) Describe one change in the electrolyte during the experiment.
items.answer: (a) Na⁺, OH⁻, H⁺ (b) 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (c) 4OH⁻ → O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ (d) the concentration of the dissolved compound changes as ions are discharged

items.stem: A technician in Madrid electrolyses concentrated aqueous potassium bromide with carbon electrodes and collects the products. (a) Name the product at the cathode and explain why it forms. (b) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the cathode. (c) Write the half-equation for the reaction at the anode. (d) Describe a test to identify the product at the anode. (e) Describe one change in the electrolyte during the experiment.
items.answer: (a) hydrogen: the metal is more reactive than hydrogen, so H⁺ ions are discharged instead (b) 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ (c) 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ (d) the solution near the anode turns orange/brown (e) potassium hydroxide solution remains
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark product; 1 mark reason [2] (b) [1] (c) [1] (d) [1] (e) [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct half-equation for the formation of iron at the cathode from Fe³⁺ ions?
items.answer: Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe
items.markingKey: Reduction at cathode: Fe³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Fe (charges balance).

items.stem: Lucas tried to electroplate a steel bolt with zinc but connected the steel bolt to the positive terminal. Explain why this would not work well and how to correct it.
items.answer: The steel bolt must be the cathode (negative) so that Zn²⁺ ions gain electrons and deposit on it; as the anode it would be oxidised instead.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: problem explained; 1 mark: correction [2]

items.stem: A iron door handle is to be electroplated with copper. Name the anode, the cathode and a suitable electrolyte.
items.answer: anode: copper; cathode: iron door handle; electrolyte: aqueous copper(II) sulfate
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [3]

items.stem: Aisha wants to electroplate a brass medal with silver. Describe the set-up: name the anode, the cathode and the electrolyte, and write the half-equations at each electrode.
items.answer: anode: silver; cathode: the brass medal; electrolyte: aqueous silver nitrate. Cathode: Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag; anode: Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻
items.markingKey: anode silver [1]; cathode brass medal [1]; electrolyte silver nitrate [1]; Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag [1]; anode half-equation [1]

items.stem: Sofia sets up a cell to purify a bar of impure copper by electrolysis. (a) Name the anode, cathode and electrolyte used. (b) Write the half-equation at the cathode. (c) Suggest why very pure copper is needed for wiring.
items.answer: (a) anode: impure copper; cathode: pure copper; electrolyte: aqueous copper(II) sulfate (b) Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (c) impurities reduce electrical conductivity
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [3] (b) [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Explain why a fuel cell is described as converting chemical energy directly into electrical energy.
items.answer: The redox reaction between hydrogen and oxygen transfers electrons through an external circuit, rather than burning the fuel to produce heat and then motion.

items.stem: The government of a country is deciding whether to build hydrogen filling stations in Toronto. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells compared with petrol or diesel engines.
items.answer: Advantage: fuel cells are more efficient at converting chemical energy to electrical energy. Disadvantage: fuel cells are expensive (they contain costly catalysts such as platinum).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: advantage; 1 mark: explanation; 1 mark: disadvantage with explanation [3]

items.stem: Ines compares a hydrogen fuel cell car with a petrol car in Cairo. Data: range on a full tank – fuel cell 650 km, petrol 600 km; refuelling time – fuel cell 5 min, petrol 5 min; CO₂ emitted while driving – fuel cell 0 g/km, petrol 180 g/km; purchase price – fuel cell $55,000, petrol $25,000; filling stations in the city – hydrogen 8, petrol 800. Give one advantage and one disadvantage of the fuel cell car shown by the data, and state which car you would choose.
items.answer: Fuel cell: no CO₂ or other pollutants when driving (only water), but costs $30,000 more, although it has 50 km more range and there are only 8 hydrogen filling stations; hydrogen may be made from fossil fuels. Petrol: cheaper, convenient, but emits CO₂ (climate change) plus CO, NOx and particulates. A justified conclusion either way.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: one advantage from the data; 1 mark: one disadvantage from the data; 1 mark: conclusion with reason [3]
